text.title: How Suspension Bridges Carry Loads
text.body:
A suspension bridge hangs its road deck from cables rather than resting it on a series of supports. Two or more tall towers hold up the main cables, which pass over the tops of the towers and are fixed at each end to massive anchorages buried in rock or concrete. Thinner vertical cables, called hangers, connect the main cables to the deck below.

The design works because steel cables are extremely strong in tension, that is, when they are pulled. The weight of the deck and its traffic pulls down on the hangers, which transfer the load to the main cables. The main cables carry this tension to the anchorages, while the towers are pressed downward in compression and pass the force into their foundations.

Because the cables do most of the work, suspension bridges can span far greater distances than beam or arch bridges. However, their light, flexible decks can move in strong wind. The collapse of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in 1940, which twisted violently in a moderate wind, taught engineers to build stiffer decks and to test models in wind tunnels.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 1, what is the function of the hangers?
options: They fix the main cables to the anchorages.
They link the main cables to the road deck.
They pass over the tops of the towers.
They hold the towers firmly in the rock.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says 'hangers, connect the main cables to the deck below'.

questions.prompt: The word 'massive' in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to
options: hidden
ancient
smooth
enormous
questions.explanation: Anchorages that hold the main cables 'buried in rock or concrete' are very large and heavy, so 'massive' means 'enormous'.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, which of the following is NOT true of the towers?
options: They are pulled upward by the hangers.
They hold up the main cables.
They are under compression.
They pass force into their foundations.
questions.explanation: The towers 'hold up the main cables' and 'are pressed downward in compression and pass the force into their foundations'; the hangers pull on the main cables, not upward on the towers.

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention the Tacoma Narrows Bridge?
options: To show that suspension bridges are cheap to build
To give an example of a bridge with very long cables
To illustrate a weakness that changed bridge design
To explain why steel is strong when it is pulled
questions.explanation: It follows 'their light, flexible decks can move in strong wind', and its collapse 'taught engineers to build stiffer decks'.

options: They move more in strong wind than suspension bridges.

They depend mainly on cables that are in tension.
questions.explanation: Suspension bridges 'can span far greater distances than beam or arch bridges', so those types are less suited to very wide crossings.

text.title: How Honeybees Share the Location of Food
text.body:
Honeybees live in large colonies, and they need a great deal of nectar and pollen to survive. Some of the bees in a colony work as foragers. Their job is to fly out, find flowers and bring food back to the hive. When a forager finds a good source of food, she does not keep the information to herself. Instead, she tells her sisters with a dance.

If the flowers are close to the hive, the bee performs a round dance, moving in small circles. This tells other bees that food is nearby, but not in which direction. If the flowers are farther away, she performs a waggle dance. She runs in a straight line while shaking her body, then circles back and repeats the run. The direction of the run shows the direction of the food compared with the sun, and the length of the waggle shows how far away the food is.

Other bees follow the dancer closely and smell the flowers on her body. Then they leave the hive and fly to the food themselves.

options: To build new parts of the hive
To protect the colony from danger
To care for young bees in the hive
To find food and carry it back
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says foragers 'fly out, find flowers and bring food back to the hive'.

questions.explanation: 'A good source of food' is a place with a good supply of food, here the flowers the forager finds.

options: The exact direction of the food
That food is close to the hive

That the hive is in danger
questions.explanation: The round dance 'tells other bees that food is nearby, but not in which direction'.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, which of the following is NOT shown by the waggle dance?
options: The kind of flower that was found
The direction of the food
How far away the food is

questions.explanation: The run shows 'the direction of the food compared with the sun' and the waggle shows 'how far away the food is'; the type of flower is not shown by the dance.

They only visit flowers near the hive.
questions.explanation: The followers 'smell the flowers on her body' before flying out, so they use smell together with the dance.

text.title: Mechanical Clocks and the Measurement of Time in Medieval Europe
text.body:
Before the late thirteenth century, Europeans measured time with sundials, which were useless at night or under cloud, and with water clocks, which froze in winter and required constant attention. Daily life was organised around unequal hours: daylight was divided into twelve parts, so an hour in June was considerably longer than one in December.

The decisive innovation, which appeared around 1300, was the verge-and-foliot escapement. A falling weight turned a set of gears, but the escapement repeatedly halted and released this motion, dividing it into regular beats. Early mechanical clocks were inaccurate by modern standards, often gaining or losing a quarter of an hour a day, yet they ran continuously regardless of season or weather.

Because a mechanism beats at a constant rate, clocks encouraged the adoption of equal hours. Towns installed large clocks on churches and town halls, and their bells came to regulate when markets opened and when labourers began and ended work. Historians have therefore argued that the clock did not merely record time; it gradually reshaped how people experienced it.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 1, why was an hour in June longer than an hour in December?
options: Water clocks ran faster in warm weather.
Sundials were used only in summer months.
Clocks gained time during long summer days.
Daylight was always split into twelve parts.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says 'daylight was divided into twelve parts, so an hour in June was considerably longer than one in December'.

questions.prompt: The word 'decisive' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
options: crucial
costly
careful
sudden
questions.explanation: The escapement is presented as the innovation that made mechanical clocks work, so 'decisive' means 'crucial'.

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention that early clocks often gained or lost a quarter of an hour a day?
options: To argue that sundials remained more reliable
To explain why towns put clocks on churches
To admit a weakness before stating an advantage
To show that the escapement came much later
questions.explanation: The inaccuracy is followed by 'yet they ran continuously regardless of season or weather', so it is a concession before the key advantage.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, all of the following were problems with earlier ways of measuring time EXCEPT
options: They divided motion into irregular beats.
They could not be used at night.
They could freeze in cold weather.
They needed to be watched constantly.
questions.explanation: Sundials were 'useless at night' and water clocks 'froze in winter and required constant attention'; dividing motion into beats describes the later escapement, not an earlier problem.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from the passage about working life before equal hours became common?
options: Markets usually opened only after dark.
Labourers worked equal minutes all year.
Town halls were not yet given bells.
Working time varied with the season.
questions.explanation: Under 'unequal hours' an hour changed length between June and December, and only later did clock bells regulate 'when labourers began and ended work', so working time must have varied seasonally.

tasks.context: Listen to part of a talk in an archaeology class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Okay, today I want to look at a dating method that archaeologists love, because it can be accurate to a single year. It's called dendrochronology, or tree-ring dating. In regions with a clear growing season, a tree adds one ring of wood every year. But the rings aren't all the same width. In a good year, with plenty of rain, a tree grows a wide ring. In a dry year, the ring is narrow. So trees of the same species growing in the same region end up with the same pattern of wide and narrow rings, a bit like a barcode. Now, researchers start with living trees, where they know the date of the outermost ring. Then they find older timbers, say beams from old buildings, whose inner rings overlap with the outer rings of the living trees. By linking these overlaps, they've built master sequences that go back thousands of years. So, if you dig up a wooden beam, or, um, a plank from a shipwreck, you measure its rings and slide its pattern along the master sequence until it matches. There's one catch, though. If a carpenter trimmed off the outer layers of the wood, you only get the earliest possible date the tree was cut down, not the exact year. That's why archaeologists get quite excited when the bark edge has survived.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: Why trees grow faster in wet years

Why bark protects trees from dry weather
questions.explanation: The professor introduces 'tree-ring dating' and explains how ring patterns are matched to a master sequence.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, why do trees in the same region share a ring pattern?

They experience the same yearly weather.
They are cut down at the same age.
questions.explanation: Ring width depends on rainy or dry years, so trees in the same region record the same sequence of conditions.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor compare ring patterns to a barcode?

tasks.context: Listen to part of a talk in a meteorology class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Let's turn to something you've all walked through: fog. Fog is really just a cloud that forms at ground level. It's made of tiny water droplets hanging in the air. And it forms when air cools to its dew point, the temperature at which it can't hold all its water vapour, so some of that vapour condenses. Now, there are a few ways air can cool like that. The most common is radiation fog. On a clear, calm night, the ground loses heat into the sky quickly, and it chills the layer of air just above it. By dawn, that air may reach its dew point, and you get fog, often settling in valleys, because cold air is heavier and drains downhill. Notice I said clear and calm. If there are clouds, they act like a blanket and keep the ground warmer. And a strong wind mixes the cold air with warmer air above, so the fog doesn't form. The second type is advection fog. Here, warm, moist air moves sideways over a cold surface, like cold ocean water. The coast of California gets a lot of this in summer. Radiation fog usually clears by midmorning, once the sun warms the ground. Advection fog, though, can hang around for days, as long as that moist air keeps flowing in.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: Why fog is dangerous for drivers
How clouds keep the ground warm at night
The conditions that cause fog to form
Why California has a dry summer climate
questions.explanation: The professor defines fog, explains the dew point and describes how radiation fog and advection fog form.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, why does radiation fog often collect in valleys?
options: Valleys have more rivers and lakes.
Cold air is heavy and flows downhill.
Wind is strongest on the valley floor.
Clouds rarely form above valleys.
questions.explanation: He says fog settles in valleys 'because cold air is heavier and drains downhill'.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor say, 'Notice I said clear and calm'?
options: To correct a mistake he made earlier
To introduce the second type of fog
To suggest that fog is rare in winter
To stress two conditions radiation fog needs
questions.explanation: He then explains that clouds keep the ground warm and wind mixes the air, so both conditions are needed for radiation fog.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about a cloudy, windy night?
options: Radiation fog is unlikely to form.
Advection fog will last for days.
The ground will cool faster than usual.
The air will reach its dew point early.
questions.explanation: Clouds keep the ground warmer and strong wind stops cold air from settling, so neither condition for radiation fog is met.

tasks.context: Listen to part of a talk in an agricultural history class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Today we're talking about crop rotation. That means growing different crops in a field from one year to the next. Why do farmers do this? Well, if you plant the same crop in the same place every year, the soil slowly loses the nutrients that crop needs. Pests and diseases also build up. In medieval Europe, many villages used a three-field system. One field grew wheat or rye, which was planted in the autumn. A second field grew crops like oats, barley, peas or beans, which were planted in the spring. And the third field was left empty, or fallow, so the soil could rest. Each year, the crops moved to the next field. Then, in the 1700s, farmers in England improved this with a four-field system. They grew wheat, turnips, barley and clover. Clover actually adds nitrogen to the soil, so no field had to stay empty. And the turnips fed farm animals during the winter. So farmers got more food from the same land.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: Why farmers moved from villages to cities
How to grow wheat in cold weather
Which crops medieval farmers liked best
How farmers changed crops to protect the soil
questions.explanation: The professor defines crop rotation and explains how the three-field and four-field systems kept soil healthy.

questions.prompt: In the three-field system, what happened to the third field?
options: It was left empty to rest.
It was used to grow turnips.
It was planted in the autumn.
It was used to keep animals.
questions.explanation: The professor says the third field 'was left empty, or fallow, so the soil could rest'.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, why was clover useful?
options: Animals preferred it to turnips.
It added nitrogen to the soil.
It grew quickly in the winter.
It kept pests away from wheat.
questions.explanation: He says, 'Clover actually adds nitrogen to the soil.'

questions.prompt: What was one advantage of the four-field system?
options: Farmers needed fewer animals.
Fields did not need any planting.
More of the land produced food each year.
Farmers could stop growing wheat.
questions.explanation: With clover, 'no field had to stay empty', so farmers 'got more food from the same land'.

tasks.context: Listen to part of a talk in a film studies class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: So, we often say that sound arrived in 1927, with The Jazz Singer. And that's fair, as long as we're careful. First, silent films were never actually silent. Cinemas hired pianists, sometimes whole orchestras, to play along. What The Jazz Singer offered was synchronised sound: songs and a few spoken lines recorded on discs that played in step with the picture. Audiences were thrilled, and within about three years the major Hollywood studios had largely stopped making silent features. But here's what tends to get left out. Early sound actually made films worse in some ways, at least for a while. Cameras were noisy, so they had to be shut inside soundproof booths, and they could barely move. Microphones were crude, so actors had to stay close to them, sometimes hidden in a vase of flowers. The result? A lot of stiff, stagey scenes, after directors had spent years making the camera fluid and expressive. There was a business cost, too. A silent film could be sold abroad simply by swapping the title cards for another language. A talking picture suddenly had a language barrier. Some studios even reshot films with different casts for different markets. So was sound progress? Eventually, yes. Once cameras were silenced and microphones moved onto booms, filmmakers got their mobility back. But the transition wasn't the straight line upward it's often made out to be.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: Why The Jazz Singer failed commercially
How orchestras accompanied early films
Why studios preferred silent films to talkies
The drawbacks that came with the shift to sound
questions.explanation: After a brief introduction, most of the talk covers 'what tends to get left out': the artistic and business problems of early sound.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor mention pianists and orchestras?
options: To explain how sound was recorded on discs
To show that silent films already had sound
To argue that live music was too expensive
To describe the plot of The Jazz Singer
questions.explanation: They support her point that 'silent films were never actually silent' because live music played along.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, why were many early sound scenes stiff?
options: Actors had never performed on a stage.
Directors preferred to film outdoors.
Noisy cameras were shut inside booths.
Title cards kept interrupting the action.
questions.explanation: Cameras 'had to be shut inside soundproof booths, and they could barely move', which produced stagey scenes.

questions.prompt: What is the professor's attitude toward the common view that sound was simple progress?
options: She thinks it oversimplifies what happened.
She thinks it is completely mistaken.
She thinks it ignores the silent-era actors.
She thinks it overstates the costs involved.
questions.explanation: She agrees sound was progress 'eventually' but says it 'wasn't the straight line upward it's often made out to be'.

tasks.context: Listen to part of a talk in an economics class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Picture a fireworks display over a town. Once those fireworks go up, anyone in town can watch, whether they chipped in or not. That's what economists call a public good. It has two features. It's non-excludable, so you can't easily stop non-payers from enjoying it. And it's non-rival, meaning my watching doesn't leave less for you. Compare that with a sandwich, which is neither. Now, here's the problem. If you'll get the show anyway, why pay? Economists call this free riding. And if enough people reason that way, the organisers can't cover their costs and the show doesn't happen, even though almost everyone would have happily paid a little. So the market, left alone, tends to supply too little of these goods.

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: So is that why governments pay for things like street lights?

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Exactly. Taxes are one solution: everyone pays, so nobody rides free. But it's not the only one. Small communities often manage through social pressure, since it's hard to free ride when your neighbours know you didn't contribute. And the textbook example, the lighthouse, turns out to be messier than it looks. The economist Ronald Coase pointed out that in Britain, many lighthouses were funded by fees charged to ships at nearby ports. So a supposedly pure public good was paid for privately, by linking it to something you could exclude people from.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How towns organise their fireworks displays
Why public goods tend to be undersupplied
How Coase designed lighthouses in Britain
Why taxes on shipping were first introduced
questions.explanation: The professor defines public goods, explains free riding and says markets 'supply too little of these goods', then discusses solutions.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor mention a sandwich?
options: To give an example of a non-rival good
To show how free riding affects food prices
To explain what social pressure means
To contrast a private good with a public one
questions.explanation: A sandwich is 'neither' non-excludable nor non-rival, so it is the opposite case to the fireworks.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor mention lighthouses funded by port fees?
options: To show that public goods can be funded privately
To prove that lighthouses are pure public goods
To argue that governments built most lighthouses
To explain why ships refused to pay for lighthouses
questions.explanation: He says 'a supposedly pure public good was paid for privately', which challenges the textbook example.

questions.prompt: What does the professor imply about a fireworks show that gets cancelled?
options: Most people in the town did not want it.
The organisers set the ticket price too low.
It could have been paid for if all contributed.
Social pressure stopped people from paying.
questions.explanation: He says it fails 'even though almost everyone would have happily paid a little', so the money existed if everyone contributed.

items.prompt: How much longer will you be working tonight?
items.explanation: I need about an hour to finish the report. "Hour" begins with a vowel sound, so it takes "an"; "the report" refers to a specific report both speakers know about.

items.prompt: Hello? Can you hear me clearly?
items.explanation: Sorry, I can hardly hear you because of the wind. The adverb "hardly" goes between the modal verb and the main verb.

items.prompt: Excuse me, I'm new to this neighborhood.
items.explanation: Could you tell me where the nearest bus stop is? In an indirect question the subject comes before the verb (not "where is the nearest bus stop").

items.prompt: Why did you join the cooking club?
items.explanation: I'm interested in learning how to bake bread. After a preposition ("in") we use the -ing form, and "how" is followed by the to-infinitive.

items.prompt: Should I take the coast road to the airport?
items.explanation: I wouldn't. It's not nearly as fast as the highway. The pattern is "not nearly as + adjective + as", with "nearly" directly after "not".

items.prompt: Who is that woman talking to the manager?
items.explanation: She's the designer who created our company's new logo. The relative clause starts with "who" directly after the noun it describes.

items.prompt: Is the team meeting still on for this afternoon?
items.explanation: No, it has been put off until next Friday. This is the present perfect passive (has been + past participle) of the phrasal verb "put off" (postpone).

items.prompt: Did you go to the open-air concert last weekend?
items.explanation: No, but I would have gone if I had heard about it. In a third conditional the main clause uses "would have + past participle" and the if-clause uses the past perfect.

items.prompt: Why was Lena so upset after work yesterday?
items.explanation: She realized that she had lost her keys on the bus. The past perfect ("had lost") shows that losing the keys happened before she realized it.

items.prompt: How was dinner at the new Thai restaurant?
items.explanation: Not only was the food delicious, but the prices were also reasonable. After a sentence-initial "Not only", the verb comes before the subject (inversion).

tasks.intro: Hello, and thanks for taking the time to talk with me. Today I'd like to ask you some questions about daily routines and how people manage their time.

questions.text: To begin, could you describe what a typical weekday morning looks like for you?
Tell me about a time when you had too many things to do and not enough time. What happened, and how did you handle it?
Compared with ten years ago, do you think people today have more free time or less? And how do you think that will change in the future?
Some companies are trying a four-day working week, where employees work fewer days but longer hours. Do you think this is a good idea for workers and businesses? Why or why not?
